question: to the Commission Nikolaos Anadiotis (NI) Subject:

The death of English-language teacher Sofia Christidou in Thessaloniki, following a haemorrhagic stroke, has sparked public debate over alleged complaints of bullying by pupils and the way in which the educational authorities handled her case. According to reports, the Sworn Administrative Inquiry is examining 16 documents, complaints and the teacher's referral to a health committee, while relatives attribute the deterioration of her health to behaviour and institutional inaction12. The incident highlights a broader issue of protecting teachers from violence, harassment and psychosocial risks in the workplace, which fall within the scope of health and safety at work under Directive 89/391/EEC34. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission have comparable data on incidents of violence, harassment or intimidation against teachers in Member States?
How does the Commission assess the implementation of Directive 89/391/EEC on the prevention of psychosocial risks and violence by third parties in public education?
Does the Commission intend to propose guidelines or a European mechanism for recording and preventing such incidents and supporting teachers who encounter them?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.7.2026) The Commission (Eurostat) collects data on reported non-fatal and fatal accidents at work. In the education sector in Greece, no fatal1 accidents were reported for 2014-2023, while the number of non-fatal cases2 rose from 42 in 2021 to 54 in 2023. According to the 2024 European Survey of Enterprises on New and Emerging Risks (ESENER) survey3, 85% of respondents in the education sector in Greece reported having to deal with difficult customers, patients or pupils. The Commission is working with stakeholders to find solutions for this complex topic. The Framework Directive on Safety and Health at Work4 covers all occupational risks and applies to all sectors of activity, including education, and it is up to Member States to properly and effectively transpose it. The Commission regularly undertakes a review to assess the practical implementation at the national level of this and 23 related EU directives. The results of the latest review, covering the period 2018 to 2022, are expected to be published later in 2026. As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is carrying out a review of the Workplace Directive5 and Display Screen Directive6. Possible EU action would strive to reconcile the need to improve worker protection in light of the digital transition, while avoiding unnecessary burden on companies and simplifying the legislation. Issues to be addressed would include better addressing the psychosocial risks, including in education. The Commission supports teacher safety by promoting safe, inclusive school environments and whole-school measures to prevent school violence, bullying and harassment7. The envisaged EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda announced in the Union of Skills would also cover teachers’ working conditions.
